## Scene 2

The first physical sign of the approaching front was invisible — only the instruments could see it, the way you can't see a cold front arrive on Earth but the barometer drops and your joints ache hours before the rain.

*Mission AI: "Particulate density has doubled since last update. Wind speeds: forty-two kilometers per hour. Direction: east-southeast. Solar panel array alpha receiving initial particulate coating. Output reduction: three percent."*

Three percent sounded small until Arun explained what it meant on the exterior walkway, a portable sensor in his gloved hand aimed at the nearest solar panel. The panel looked clean — still reflecting the thin sunlight back in a pale glint. But the sensor told a different story. Dust particles, invisible to the eye, were already settling on the surface. Like breath on glass. You could feel it before you could see it.

"This isn't the problem yet," Arun said through comms. "We've got a thin film already forming. Right now it's negligible. But the film gets thicker, and it doesn't wash off. No rain to clean this. There's only what we can do mechanically."

Tomas was working on the loader fleet — three exterior robotic arms mounted on rails along the side of the main module. The loaders were their workhorses. Two were parked under a deployable awning. The third had to stay outside.

"We should park the third one," Imani said over comms from inside ops.

Tomas shook his head. "We don't have time to reconfigure the whole exterior workflow. The habitat module needs its anchoring struts bolted down before the storm. If we take the loader offline now, we lose twelve hours of exterior work and we'll be racing the front to finish. Not a good trade."

Arun appeared beside him in his pressure suit. "Tomas is right. We keep the loader running. But we can at least point it into the wind."

They worked together, manhandling the loader's positioning controls, rotating the robotic arm on its rail so that its joints and optical sensors faced the least direct exposure. The loader protested mechanically — its rails groaned — but it moved, sluggishly, and locked into position with a sound like clearing a throat.

"Better than nothing," Arun said.

Inside, Jonah's 3D printer ran nonstop, extruding thermoplastic gaskets, adhesive tape strips, custom-fit covers for external sensor housings. His hands moved fast, pulling parts off the bed as soon as they cooled, stacking them on a cart that he pushed from bay to bay like a supply runner in a field hospital.

Elena coordinated from ops, her voice calm and steady on the comms, calling out priorities and adjusting assignments as the clock ticked down. She had the look of a pilot in final approach — eyes fixed, hands moving with economy, nothing wasted.

"Mission AI, what's our current power balance?"

*Mission AI: "Solar: one hundred percent nominal output. Reactor: one hundred percent. Battery reserves: ninety-eight percent of capacity. Total margin: nominal."*

"Good," Elena said. "Because it won't be soon."

The final twelve hours were a blur of exterior runs, teams in pressure suits moving in shifts to apply protective covers, tighten seals, and position loaders in defensible stances. Arun made each run himself when he could, inspecting every connection with the paranoid thoroughness of someone who knew that one overlooked gasket could become a catastrophe six weeks later.

Imani stayed in ops, running power simulations. The models all said the same thing: at peak storm density, solar generation would drop by at least seventy percent. The reactor radiator efficiency would degrade as dust coated the fins. They would survive on margins — thinner and thinner margins with every passing hour.

"Mission AI," she said during one run, "what happens if we lose the reactor radiator to full coating?"

*Mission AI: "Full coating of reactor radiators would require an emergency reactor shutdown within approximately four hours of coating onset. Without reactor output, solar generation must supply all base power. At peak storm density, available solar generation is insufficient to maintain life support, communications, and minimal heating systems. Estimated survival window without manual radiator cleaning: approximately fourteen hours."*

Imani swallowed. "So the radiator has to stay clear."

*Mission AI: "Correct. Rotor cleaning systems can maintain radiator surface to approximately sixty percent efficiency if particulate settling rate remains within modeled parameters. If settling rate exceeds the model —"*

"Yeah, I know," she said quietly. "We're dead."

The final exterior run before the storm hit was Arun and Tomas together. They checked every seal, confirmed every shutter, verified that all six solar panel arrays were braced. The panels wouldn't be damaged by wind — the atmosphere was too thin for that. But the mounting hardware had to hold, and the angle adjustments had to be set correctly to minimize dust deposition. It was a compromise: steeper angles shed more dust but captured less light under already-reduced conditions. Flatter angles caught more light but collected more dust. Arun chose an intermediate angle and called it the best bad option he could find.

They were back inside when the front arrived.

---

## Scene 3

The storm did not announce itself with a dramatic wall of darkness. No towering shelf cloud, no roiling black horizon swallowing the world. The atmosphere on Mars was too thin for spectacle. The dust came quietly — a thinning of light, a yellowing of the air quality sensors, a gradual dimming of the landscape outside the viewports as if someone were turning down a rheostat on the sun.

The first significant coating arrived three hours after the front passed over the base. Imani watched it on the external cameras: a film of ochre powder settling slowly onto every exposed surface, like fine snow falling in slow motion. There was no wind to drive it horizontally, none of the cinematic fury. The dust descended with the indifference of gravity, settling on solar panels, optics, joints and hinges, reactor radiators — every surface, indiscriminately, without discrimination or mercy.

*Mission AI: "Solar panel array alpha output has dropped to seventy-two percent of nominal. Array bravo: sixty-eight percent. All arrays showing particulate accumulation."*

Arun watched the numbers cascade across his monitor with his chin resting in his hand. This was the part he had feared. The storm itself was survivable. It was the settling — the way the dust clung to surfaces and refused to leave — that made a single event into a cascading problem. The longer the storm lasted, the thicker the coating. The thicker the coating, the less power. The less power, the harder it was to run the systems that could clean the coating.

Outside, the third loader was already in trouble.

Tomas saw it first on the external camera feed — one of the loader's arm joints had stopped moving. The elbow joint was encased in a thin crust of dust, the movement rails packed with fine particles that had worked their way into the microscopic gaps between metal surfaces.

"Loader three is seizing," Tomas said. "Elbow joint rails are clogged."

"Can remote commands clear it?" Elena asked.

Tomas ran through the motion commands. The loader's arm twitched — the joint tried to move and failed, the motor whining audibly through the camera microphone. Twitch. Whine. Stop. Twitch. Whine. Stop. The sound was agonizing, like a knee joint grinding bone on bone.

"No. It's mechanically blocked. Dust has gotten past the seals. We'll have to go out and clean it manually."

"When?"

Tomas looked at the feed. The landscape was dim, the air thick with suspended dust. "Not now. We wait for a lull. If there is one."

Imani pulled up the weather model. "Brief density decrease at hour twenty-two. About a two-hour window before the front thickens again for the peak."

"Then we wait for hour twenty-two," Elena decided. "Tomas, prepare the cleaning kit now. Arun, I want you with him."

Arun's mind was already on the reactor radiators, because while the loader was annoying, the radiators were existential. If the radiators failed, everything failed.

The radiator fins were thin — thinner than a fingernail — and stacked close together. Dust settling between those fins was almost impossible to remove without physically extracting each fin stack. The built-in wipers could only clear the top surfaces. Between the fins, the dust accumulated in the shadows, unseen, building up like silt in a riverbed. Arun had chosen simpler wipers during design — weight versus effectiveness, complexity versus reliability. In the end, they had accepted the risk of inter-fin accumulation.

"Misison AI, what's the current radiator efficiency?"

*Mission AI: "Radiator thermal dissipation at seventy-nine percent of nominal. Dust accumulation on fin surfaces: moderate. Wiper system operational. Projected efficiency at peak storm density: approximately fifty-two percent, assuming wiper effectiveness remains constant."*

Fifty-two percent. Enough to keep the reactor running, but barely. No safety margin. Arun did the mental math: fifty-two percent meant the reactor had to throttle. Throttled output was still enough for life support and minimal systems — but only just. If solar dropped below thirty percent at the same time, they'd be shutting down nonessential systems.

The storm deepened. Outside the viewports, the world went from amber to ochre to a flat, featureless brown. Horizon vanished. The sky was neither sky nor cloud but a uniform haze that absorbed light without reflecting it. The sun became a coin-sized dimmer spot in the haze — present but muted.

Hour twenty-two arrived. The storm briefly thinned.

Tomas and Arun went outside.

They found the loader exactly as the cameras had shown — the elbow joint encased in a crust of oxidized iron dust, the movement rails packed so thoroughly that Tomas could barely see the gap where the lubricant should have been. He worked methodically, compressed gas to blow out surface accumulation, small brush into the rails, more gas, then silicone-based lubricant. The dust clung. It clung to the brush. It clung to the gas stream. It clung to the lubricant before the lubricant reached the metal surface.

"It's like cleaning with molasses," Tomas muttered.

"Just keep working," Arun said. He checked every visible joint, every seal, every connection he could reach while they were both suited up. He found dust inside a connector housing that should have been sealed. He found it packed into the groove of a hatch seal installed six weeks ago. He found it in places that had no business having dust, places that had no obvious path of entry.

It found every way in.

They freed the loader after forty minutes. The joint moved again — hesitant at first, then smooth as the lubricant found the microscopic imperfections of the metal surface.

"Good enough," Elena said over comms. "Come inside."

The second run was Arun and Imani, forty minutes later, for the reactor radiators. Arun needed to manually check the fin surfaces and clear any accumulation the wipers had missed. He had suspected he would need to do this. He just hadn't wanted to confirm it this soon.

The radiator array extended from the side of the reactor module like a row of thin metallic ribs — eleven fin stacks, each about a meter tall, separated by gaps barely wide enough to fit fingers. Dust had settled on the top surfaces, visible as a thin, rust-colored film. Arun ran the wiper system from a manual control. The wipers dragged the dust into collection grooves. Most of it came clear.

But beneath the top surfaces, in the narrow gaps between fins, the dust had settled in the dead air — a layer maybe a millimeter deep, packed into the space like sediment in a canyon.

"Can't reach that," Imani said, peering into the gap.

"Not today. If the accumulation stays below three millimeters, the wipers will handle what they can and it won't kill us."

"And if it goes above three millimeters?"

Arun measured another gap, then another. Consistent — dust in every gap, varying from nearly nothing to about two millimeters in the worst spot.

"Then we'll have to think of something else."

The storm sealed itself around the base like a fist closing.

---

## Scene 4

*Mission AI: "Hour twenty-eight of the storm event. Solar panel array alpha output: twenty-nine percent. Array bravo: twenty-six percent. Array charlie: twenty-three percent. Average array efficiency: twenty-six percent. Total solar generation: below minimum threshold for full base operations. Battery reserves: seventy-four percent. Declining at approximately one-point-two percent per hour."*

Elena stood in the center of the operations module looking at the master display without seeing it. Her eyes were somewhere else, calculating, weighing.

"Mission AI, show me the full power budget."

The display shifted to a waterfall chart — every system the base drew power from listed in priority order. Most of the bars were green. A few were touching the red. One — the reactor radiator wiper system — had already crossed it.

"Reactor is down to sixty-one percent thermal output," Arun said. "Radiator effectiveness is at fifty-seven percent. The wipers can't keep up with the settling rate in this density. We're accumulating approximately point-three millimeters per hour on the fin surfaces. At that rate, we reach three millimeters in about ten hours."

Ten hours from now, the reactor would hit its thermal limit and emergency shutdown protocols would initiate automatically. The AI would trip the breakers, shut down the fission core, and leave them running on batteries and whatever solar they could scrape from dust-coated panels.

"How long can we survive on batteries and reduced solar?" Elena asked.

Arun had done this math a hundred times during planning and training. But the numbers in the simulation hadn't felt real. The numbers in front of him now felt like a countdown.

"Battery reserves at seventy-four percent. Drain rate at current power budget: about one point two percent per hour. That's about sixty hours from now. But if the solar keeps dropping below twenty percent, that drops to about forty hours."

Forty to sixty hours of life support, minimal heating, and essential systems. After that, the air scrubbers would stop. Then the heaters. Then communications.

And they would freeze.

"Can we extend the battery life?"

"We can shut down nonessential systems. Kill the science lab — save five percent. Shut down the fab bay — save another eight. Cut the hot water — marginal. Reduce habitat temperature by five degrees — save six percent. Total savings: roughly twenty percent. That extends the battery window by approximately ten to twelve hours."

"Do it. Strip the base to minimum viable."

Systems went dark one by one — the fabrication bay powered down with a low whine and a shower of sparks from an unfinished print job. The science instruments powered off. The habitat temperature dropped steadily, and everyone felt it immediately: the recycled air grew bitingly cold, and the floor plates transmitted the deep cold of the Martian surface through the insulation.

Everyone put on their thermal layers. Elena was first — both practical and symbolic. If the commander was going to be cold, everyone would follow.

Imani watched the power budget shift as the green bars shrank. The battery drain rate slowed from one-point-two percent per hour to about point-nine. It bought time, but not enough.

*Mission AI: "Storm density peak is approximately six hours away. Current particulate density: forty-seven micrograms per cubic meter. Peak predicted density: approximately seventy-three micrograms per cubic meter. Solar generation is expected to decline further."*

Six hours to the worst of it.

Arun sat at the engineering station, his monitor displaying the reactor telemetry, the radiator temperature curves, and a live feed of the radiator fin array from a camera slowly going blind under accumulated dust. The camera showed the fin stacks, still visible through the haze, dust on the top surfaces. The gaps between fins were invisible — lost in shadow and dust.

He thought about the dust. Not as a technical problem, but as what it really was: the face of Mars. The planet didn't hate them. It didn't love them. It simply was — a world of iron oxide and basalt, of low gravity and thin air, of dust so fine it behaved as much like a fluid as a solid. Mars was neither hostile nor welcoming. It was indifferent. And indifference was more dangerous than hostility. Hostility you could fight. Indifference you just had to outlast.

Elena gathered the team in the operations module — all five of them, standing in a semicircle around the master display in the cold room. Imani could see her breath in two thermal layers. Jonah rubbed his hands together. Tomas stood with his arms crossed, jaw set.

"Here's what we know," Elena said. "The storm peaks in about six hours. At peak, our solar generation will drop to about twelve percent of normal. The reactor radiator is accumulating dust faster than the wipers can clear it. We're running on batteries for the deficit. At our current rate, we have approximately twenty-eight to thirty-four hours of power left."

Jonah was first to speak. "That's not enough."

"No," Elena agreed. "It isn't. Which means two things. First, we need the storm to clear as quickly as the models suggest. If the front moves faster, we get more solar, more power, more time. If it doesn't..."

"Second. As soon as the storm breaks, we clean the solar panels. Not some of them — all of them. Every single one of us goes outside."

Arun added, "The danger isn't the storm itself. I want everyone to understand that. The dust storm isn't dramatic. No wind that'll crush you, no lightning, no flood. It's quiet. It's powder. And it's dangerous precisely because it's not dramatic. It quietly lowers every margin at once. You've got power reserves — it eats them. You've got thermal margins — it reduces them. You've got equipment tolerances — it degrades them. Everything gets a little worse. All at the same time. And none of it is catastrophic on its own. But all of it together..."

He didn't finish the sentence. He didn't need to.

Imani felt the weight settling over the room like the dust itself — invisible, pervasive, inescapable. This was the test. Not the mission parameters or the training or the simulations. This. Standing in a cold room on another world, watching the numbers tick down, knowing that the margin between survival and failure was measured in percentages and hours.

The next hours passed in the rhythm of declining numbers.

*Mission AI: "Hour thirty-four. Solar panel array alpha output: fourteen percent. Average array efficiency: fifteen percent. Battery reserves: fifty-one percent. Radiator thermal dissipation at forty-nine percent."*

*Mission AI: "Battery reserves: thirty-four percent."*

*Mission AI: "Battery reserves: twenty-nine percent."*

*Mission AI: "Battery reserves: twenty-five percent."*

Each update was a hammer blow. Not dramatic — the AI delivered the numbers in the same flat tone it used for everything — but the repetition was its own kind of pressure.

*Mission AI: "Reactor core temperature: thirty-two degrees above nominal. Approaching soft throttle threshold."*

"Do it now," Elena said. "I'd rather throttle manually and maintain control of the rate."

Arun input the command. The reactor responded — a gentle reduction in the fission rate. The temperature curve flattened and began its slow descent. But the power output also dropped, and the battery drain rate ticked up.

*Mission AI: "Battery reserves: eighteen percent. Estimated survival window: twelve hours."*

Imani closed her eyes. Twelve hours.

Tomas had a different problem. The loader that had seized during the storm had seized again. Dust had worked its way back into the rail mechanism, packing the gap between moving parts with the same stubborn persistence as before. He couldn't justify using battery power to pressurize the airlock for a repair when the entire base was running out of power. The loader sat outside, frozen, coated in dust.

Jonah tried to keep spirits up from the dark fab bay. "I can fabricate better seals once we recover power. Until then, I'm just sitting here cold, holding a wrench."

"Get comfortable," Tomas said. "The wrench will probably be the warmest thing in that room."

Jonah's dry laugh made the cold air a fraction easier to breathe.

*Mission AI: "Storm tracking update. Particulate density is beginning to decrease. Rate of decline: approximately two micrograms per cubic meter per hour. Estimated time to fifty percent reduction in density: twelve hours. Estimated time to full clearing: approximately forty hours from now."*

Twelve hours to half density. Forty hours to clear.

*Arun's voice, barely above a whisper:* "We just have to wait."

The waiting was the hardest part. If the batteries had been failing quickly, there would have been urgency, action. Instead, there was sitting and watching and counting.

Elena moved from station to station, talking to each crew member. Not giving orders — there were none to give. Just checking in. Making sure the people in her charge were still present, still engaged, still functioning under a countdown clock.

Imani ran the weather models one more time. "If the clearing happens three hours faster than the model predicts, we recover approximately twelve percent additional solar generation. That's the difference between eighteen percent battery reserves and eighteen hours of life."

"So we need the model to be fast by three hours."

"We need the model to be slightly optimistic," Imani corrected. "Pessimism kills us. Optimism saves us."

Arun almost smiled. "That's not how science works."

"It's not science tonight. It's faith."

Elena wrote in her log. The act was small — fingers on a keyboard, words on a screen — but it was also large. Because if the power failed, the log would be the last record.

*Log entry: Commander E. Vasquez, Mission Day 47. First major weather event. Storm intensity exceeding model predictions by approximately eight percent. All crew members healthy and functioning. Morale stable. Power margins decreasing but within projected range. No panic. No false optimism. Just the work. If you're reading this, we didn't make it. Know that we tried. Know that we understood the risk. And know that Mars is not cruel. Mars is just Mars.*

She saved the log and stood up.

*Mission AI: "Battery reserves: fourteen percent."*

---

## Scene 5

The clearing took longer than anyone wanted and shorter than anyone feared.

At hour fifty-two of the storm, the particulate density dropped below twenty micrograms per cubic meter for the first time in days. The viewports showed the world emerging from the haze like a developing photograph — first the nearest rocks, then the farther ground, then the distant crater wall, all of them sharpening gradually from blurred suggestions into recognizable objects.

The sun appeared first as a brighter region in the haze, then as an outline, then as a circle — weak, washed-out, filtered through a sky the color of weak tea, but present. Real.

*Mission AI: "Solar panel array alpha output: thirty-one percent. Array bravo: twenty-nine percent. Output is recovering with decreasing particulate density. Battery reserves: fourteen percent."*

Fourteen percent. The number was terrifying and survivable in the same breath. It was the difference between *we will die* and *we had better hurry*.

"Suit up," Elena said. "We're going outside."

They emerged from the airlock into a world transformed.

The dust storm had reshaped the landscape in subtle ways. Drifts of orange dust had accumulated against the base modules, up to thirty centimeters high on the windward side. The solar panels were coated in a uniform layer that turned the once-brilliant black surfaces into dull, rust-colored rectangles. The reactor radiator fins wore a brownish film that looked like dried blood on metal.

They split into pairs and went to work.

Elena and Imani took the nearest solar panel array — six panels, each about two square meters, all caked with dust. They used soft brushes, compressed gas, and microfiber cloths. Panel one took twenty minutes. Panel two took fifteen. By panel three, they had developed a rhythm — brush, gas, wipe, inspect, repeat.

The dust was insidious. They would clear a section and think it was clean, only to find a new layer of fine particles settling almost immediately from the still-present airborne dust.

"It's like mopping during a rainstorm," Imani said, wiping a section and watching it accumulate a faint haze moments later.

"We don't have to clean them perfectly," Elena said. "We just have to clean them enough to get the batteries charging again. Twenty percent efficiency is enough to reverse the drain."

Arun and Tomas worked on the reactor radiators — delicate work, the fins fragile enough that bending one would reduce the effectiveness of the entire stack. They used compressed gas to blow accumulated dust off the top surfaces, then carefully worked brush handles into the gaps between fins. The dust came away in dry, cohesive clumps, and eventually the fin surfaces began to show through — metallic and bright.

"This is what I meant," Arun muttered between two fins. "Not the storm itself. The cleanup. The storm is just the delivery system. The damage is what it leaves behind."

Tomas nodded, concentrating on not bending a fin. "Every joint in every robot is going to need a full teardown. Dust has gotten past things I thought were sealed. We're going to be cleaning joints and replacing seals for months."

"Months," Arun agreed. "This was one storm. There will be more. We're not adapting to Mars. We're negotiating with it. And Mars doesn't negotiate."

Jonah managed supplies near the base entrance, replacing gas canisters, handing out fresh cloths and brushes. While the teams worked, he did a perimeter inspection, walking a slow circuit around the base modules. He found dust packed into the grooves of hatch seals — not enough to breach, but enough to accelerate degradation. He found dust on the antenna mounts, on the rover wheels, on every exterior surface of every piece of equipment. Nothing structurally broken. Nothing that couldn't be repaired.

But he found something that troubled him.

"Elena. Come take a look at this."

Elena finished her current panel and walked over. Jonah pointed to the water reserve tank — a large cylindrical vessel mounted to the exterior of the life support module. The tank itself was fine. But dust had coated it in a layer nearly a centimeter thick, and beneath it, along the bottom edge where the tank contacted the mounting bracket, there were moisture stains.

"Dust holds electrostatic charge," Jonah said. "That charge creates a thermal gradient. The tank surface is colder on the windward side because the dust coating is insulating it. Warmer on the leeward side. The gradient causes condensation cycles. And condensation is creating corrosion on the bracket."

Elena crouched to inspect the stain. Faint but real. Corrosion meant degradation. Degradation meant failure. The water tank mounting bracket was a single point of failure.

"How long until this becomes critical?"

"Months, maybe. But it's happening. Every storm makes it worse." Jonah straightened and looked at the tank, then at the horizon, where dust still hung in a thin haze that would never fully go away. "You know what this means, right?"

Elena stood beside him. "The imported water won't last forever. Every day we use it is a day closer to zero."

"It means we need local water," Jonah said. "We need to find it in the ground. Before the reserves become a countdown rather than a resource."

Elena held his gaze for a quiet moment. The dust settled on their visors.

"We survived the storm," she said.

"That was the easy part. This is the real work."

They finished cleaning the last of the solar panels as the sky transitioned from ochre to amber to the pale, washed-out blue that Martian noon sometimes achieved. The solar telemetry climbed steadily: thirty-eight percent, forty-two percent, forty-six percent. It was enough. Not comfortable, not safe, but enough.

They came back inside through the airlock, and the door sealed behind them with a sound that felt like the closing of a chapter.

Arun checked the reactor first, then the batteries, then life support. All stable. All recovering. All on the far side of the danger curve. He sat down at his station, took off his helmet, and ran his hand through his sweat-damp hair.

"We made it," he said.

Tomas collapsed into his chair. "Didn't we though."

Imani pulled up the weather model. The storm was gone — the red ellipse dissolved into a thin, trailing smear of amber, moving west and away, leaving the landing zone in clear conditions.

*Mission AI: "Storm event has concluded. Atmospheric conditions are returning to baseline. All systems nominal and recovering."*

Elena read the status board for the third time in as many minutes. "Reactor at eighty-nine percent. Solar at fifty-one percent and climbing. Batteries at twelve percent but charging. Life support fully operational."

She sat back and exhaled — the first unguarded breath she'd taken in days.

"Tomas, tear down every joint in every robot. Jonah, fabricate the replacement seals. Arun, post-storm report on the reactor and thermal systems by end of shift."

A chorus of affirmations.

Elena walked to the viewport. Outside, the world was recovering — the dust still present, still everywhere, but no longer actively settling. The landscape was changed. The base was changed. The crew was changed. Mars had thrown its first test at them, and they had passed — not comfortably, not gracefully, but they had passed.

She made a note in her log:

*Mission Day 50. First major storm survived. Systems intact. Crew intact. Water tank corrosion discovered — requires ongoing monitoring and a long-term solution. Next priority: find local water. The imported reserves are not infinite. We have months, not years. And every dust storm we survive brings us closer to the edge of what the reserves can support.*

She saved the log.

The reactor hummed. The batteries charged. The dust settled, as it always would, slowly and without urgency, finding every crack and gap and weakness in the thin skin they had stretched across an ancient, indifferent world.

*End of Chapter 8 — Bridge: To live here, they need local water before their imported reserves become a countdown.*
